summary: Describes an OSPF interface type that models a broadcast network as a hybrid of broadcast and point-to-multipoint. Neighbor discovery and database synchronization use the broadcast model, while router-LSAs describe the network as point-to-multipoint.

eli5.summary: A big room where everybody can hear everybody, but the map shows only the specific friendships. This lets OSPF talk the easy way and draw the careful way.

questions: what is ospf hybrid broadcast and point-to-multipoint
how does ospf handle partial connectivity on broadcast links
what is the ospf hybrid interface type
why does ospf need per neighbor costs
does the dr generate a network lsa on a hybrid interface
subtitle: An OSPF interface type that talks like a broadcast network but draws the map like point-to-multipoint.

tldr.problem: On an OSPF broadcast network a router cannot advertise a different cost to each neighbor, but treating the network as point-to-multipoint needs O(N^2) adjacencies and separate Hellos per neighbor.
tldr.mechanism: The hybrid-broadcast-and-P2MP interface type uses broadcast procedures for Hellos, DR and BDR election and database synchronization, but describes the network in router-LSAs as point-to-point links with per-neighbor costs.
tldr.outcome: Routers get accurate per-neighbor costs with broadcast efficiency, at the price of O(N^2) links in the link-state database. All routers on the network must support the type.

today: RFC 6845 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 2328 and RFC 5340.

sections.title: Two Models, Neither Quite Right
sections.content:
On a broadcast interface, OSPF (RFC 2328) uses the medium's broadcast ability for neighbor discovery. It elects a Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) to keep the link state databases of the routers on the network in sync. The limitation is that a router cannot advertise a different cost to each neighbor in its router-LSA.

Point-to-multipoint (P2MP) mode has the opposite trade-off. It lets routers advertise a different cost per neighbor, but it can require explicit configuration of neighbors, needs separate Hellos to each neighbor, and mandates adjacencies to all configured or discovered neighbors.

The RFC gives a radio network as the example: it supports true broadcast, yet the metrics between pairs of terminals can differ, for instance because of signal strength.
sections.eli5: One way to talk is shouting to the whole room, which is easy but cannot say who is closer. The other is whispering to each person one by one, which is precise but tiring.

sections.title: Why a Hybrid Helps
sections.content:
Some networks are broadcast capable but have a different cost between any pair of nodes. The cost could depend on topology and on link quality measures such as bandwidth, delay and jitter.

Treating them as OSPF broadcast networks is not accurate. Using P2MP mode describes the costs correctly but is inefficient, because it requires forming O(N^2) adjacencies for N routers. The hybrid-broadcast-and-P2MP type combines the flexibility of P2MP with the efficiency of the broadcast type.
sections.eli5: The hybrid lets everyone keep shouting across the room, but the map still records the exact distance to each person.

sections.title: How the Interface Behaves
sections.content:
Routers supporting this feature add a new value to the interface Type data item from Section 9 of RFC 2328. Most behavior is borrowed from broadcast mode:

  • Hellos: neighbor discovery and maintenance follow the broadcast procedures in RFC 2328 and RFC 5340.
  • Synchronization: routers elect a DR and BDR and use them for initial and ongoing database synchronization, as on broadcast interfaces.
  • Parameters: the Router Priority parameter applies, and so does the OSPFv3 LinkLSASuppression parameter, whose default is disabled.

The neighbor data structure gains a Neighbor Output Cost field: the cost of sending a data packet to that neighbor. It defaults to the interface output cost, and may be set by means outside this document, such as static per-neighbor configuration or any dynamic discovery supported by the network.
sections.eli5: Hellos, picking a leader and sharing news all work like a normal shouting room. Each router just also remembers how far away each neighbor is.

sections.title: How the Network Is Advertised
sections.content:
Because the interface is described in router-LSAs as a collection of point-to-point links, the DR MUST NOT generate a network-LSA for it. In OSPFv3 the DR also MUST NOT generate an intra-area-prefix-LSA for the transit network.

Routers describe the interface as for a P2MP interface (Section 12.4.1.4 of RFC 2328 and Section 4.4.3.2 of RFC 5340), with these changes to Type 1 links:

  • A router that is not the DR and has no full adjacency to the DR MUST NOT add any Type 1 links.
  • A router that is not the DR but has a full adjacency to it, and agrees with it on the DR role, MUST add a Type 1 link for each neighbor in state 2-Way or higher to which the DR's router-LSA includes a link.
  • The cost of each such link SHOULD be the Neighbor Output Cost.

In OSPFv2, routers MUST add a Type 3 link for their own IP address and a Type 3 link for the IP subnet, with cost equal to the configured output cost of the interface. In OSPFv3, routers MUST add the globally scoped IPv6 prefixes on the interface to the intra-area-prefix-LSA, with the Metric set to the configured output cost.
sections.eli5: Instead of drawing the whole room as one blob, each router draws a line to each neighbor with its own distance label. The leader does not draw a blob for the room.

sections.title: Next Hops and Graceful Restart
sections.content:
Next-hops to destinations directly connected through the interface are calculated as for a P2MP interface, per Section 16.1.1 of RFC 2328.

Two changes are needed to the graceful restart procedures in Section 2.2, item 1, of RFC 3623, so the router exits graceful restart correctly. A DR must not use the pre-restart network-LSA to work out its previous adjacencies. A router in state DROther treats an adjacency to a non-DR or non-BDR neighbor as reestablished when the neighbor reaches 2-Way.
sections.eli5: Finding the next stop works like the whisper-to-each-person model. After a restart, a router does not trust the old room-wide drawing and counts a neighbor as back once they say hello.

sections.title: Compatibility and Mismatches
sections.content:
All routers on the network must support the hybrid type for it to work. Otherwise the interface should be configured as a standard broadcast interface.

If some routers treat the interface as broadcast and others as hybrid, neighbors and adjacencies still form as on a broadcast interface. But router-LSAs and network-LSAs are built differently for the two types, so no traffic will traverse certain pairs of routers. The RFC notes this causes no persistent loops or black-holing.

To flag such mismatches, an implementation SHOULD log a message if it receives a network-LSA for a locally configured hybrid interface.
sections.eli5: If half the room draws the map one way and half the other way, some paths just do not get used. Everyone should agree on the style.

sections.title: Scalability and Management
sections.content:
Representing the network as hybrid results in O(N^2) links instead of O(N) for N routers. That increases memory use and hurts route calculation performance on all routers in the area, so designers should weigh the benefits against that cost.

For management, the RFC suggests adding a new broadcast-P2MP-hybrid value for ospfIfType/ospfv3IfType and a per-neighbor metric attribute ospfNbrMetricValue/ospfv3NbrMetricValue to the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 MIBs. That section is not normative.
sections.eli5: Drawing a line between every pair of friends makes a very big map when the room is crowded, so use this only when you need it.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no new security issues for OSPF. Security considerations for base OSPF are in RFC 2328, RFC 5340 and RFC 6506.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about beyond what OSPF already has.
